svg.desc: Comparative lamprey and primate motor hierarchy with spinal-injury timeline.
svg.text: Shared control plan, modified in each lineage: primates expanded cortical access without replacing brainstem and spinal controllers.

g.text: Two living lineages, one deeply shared plan
Neither animal is the other’s ancestor; both lineages continued to evolve after their divergence.

svg.text: shared features reveal deep vertebrate roots
modern cyclostome with its own specializations
modern mammal with expanded cortical systems
Matched levels below indicate conserved roles and circuit motifs — not identical circuitry.

g.text: Selection, brainstem command, spinal pattern generation, and feedback interact.
Cortical routes broaden access while older brainstem and spinal controllers remain active.

text.tspan: under appropriate excitation, generate alternating segmental output

svg.text: axial myotomes and a caudally traveling body wave

text.tspan: Spinal networks generate the detailed rhythm; brainstem and forebrain systems
recruit, regulate, select, and redirect it.

g.text: sensory guidance, task context, planning, and rapid correction
Spinal interneuronal, pattern, and feedback networks
combine descending input with proprioceptive, cutaneous, and local state signals
to brainstem controllers (counterpart in lamprey, panel B)
smaller direct route to selected hand and finger pools

text.tspan: and also influence distal motor circuitry.

g.text: Spinal injury removes support and regulation; the cord below the lesion then changes
Not immediate release: acute loss comes first, followed by variable recovery and reorganization.

svg.text: Timing and outcome vary with lesion level, completeness, spared pathways, and the response measured.
chronic phase: weeks to months and beyond

text.tspan: abrupt loss below the lesion of descending excitation, inhibition,

svg.text: different measures return at different rates

text.tspan: Later profiles are not one required sequence:
persistent loss of descending regulation interacts with spinal plasticity.

g.text: clonus or spasms in some patients

text.tspan: Acute spinal shock is not simple disinhibition. Later over-responsiveness reflects both loss of normal descending regulation
and spinal synaptic, interneuronal, receptor, and motor-neuron plasticity.

g.text: Evolution conserved and modified interacting controllers. Higher systems add flexible access and regulation; they neither replace lower circuits nor merely suppress them.
